How DX11 shaders are compiled while you play. GPL (default): links pipelines quickly and never skips a draw, so loading is fast and play is smooth. Hybrid: skips draws while shaders compile, but compiles each shader in full, which can cause hitches on this GPU. Async: the older background mode.

How many frames the CPU may prepare ahead of the GPU. Lower = less input lag, but the GPU then idles between frames: on this phone 1 frame let the GPU clock drop and cost FPS. Leave Default unless you are testing.

How many image buffers the game's swapchain asks for; the driver may raise or lower it to its own limits. Fewer can shorten the queue but can also stall the GPU; more is steadier. Not the same as the maximum latency above.

How the GPU clock behaves while you play. Balanced (default): the phone manages the clock and raises it only when the game really waits for the GPU. Performance: keeps the GPU at its highest clock (more heat and power; useful when the phone itself is in Balance mode, which caps the CPU). Regulated: keeps the clock above the chosen share of the maximum; it needs kernel support, otherwise it behaves like Balanced.

Who holds the frame rate to the limit. App, vsync-locked (recommended): the app releases frames in step with the display's refresh, so they stay evenly spaced. App, timer: the app uses its own timer instead of the display refresh, which can drift slightly. DXVK / VKD3D: the graphics layer limits with its own timer, which can make motion judder. App, vsync + phase (experimental): like vsync-locked, and the app also measures where frames reach the display and shifts their timing a few milliseconds so they finish mid-refresh: a small timing wobble then no longer moves a frame to the neighbouring refresh (measured at 60 Hz with FIFO). A limiter typed into Environment Variables always uses DXVK / VKD3D.
